nate-core-readiness-check-electrical-031.prompt: A PSC compressor nameplate calls for a 35 µF run capacitor; the failed part is marked 35 µF / 440 VAC. Which replacement is correct?

options.a: A 35 µF, 370 VAC part even though the original was marked 440 VAC
options.b: A 45 µF, 440 VAC part so the compressor gets extra starting torque
options.c: A 35 µF part rated 440 VAC or higher, matching the motor nameplate
options.d: Any nearby µF value if the replacement is stamped at least 370 VAC

nate-core-readiness-check-electrical-031.explanation: Match the motor’s specified microfarads (typically within about ±10% or the OEM spec) and use a voltage rating equal to or higher than the original. A 440 V part can replace 370 V, but 370 V cannot replace 440 V. Raising µF increases winding current and heat instead of adding useful start torque.

distractorExplanations.a: Dropping the voltage rating from 440 V to 370 V overstresses the dielectric even if microfarads match.
distractorExplanations.b: Extra microfarads belong to start capacitors; an oversized run capacitor overheats the start winding.
distractorExplanations.d: Nearby µF values are not interchangeable; they change winding current and can damage the motor.

nate-core-readiness-check-electrical-032.prompt: A 40 VA furnace transformer is too hot to hold after a few minutes of a cooling call. What does that usually mean?

options.a: 24 V on the secondary is supposed to run that hot under any load
options.b: An open high-pressure switch on Y has left the secondary unloaded
options.c: The 40 VA transformer is oversized for a 20 VA thermostat and relays
options.d: A shorted 24 V circuit, stuck relay, or overloaded VA rating

nate-core-readiness-check-electrical-032.explanation: A control transformer overheats when secondary current is too high: a shorted 24 V wire, a stuck relay coil, or more VA than the transformer can supply. A correctly loaded 40 VA unit runs warm, not scalding. Opening a switch removes load and cools the transformer rather than heating it.

distractorExplanations.a: 24 V is the normal secondary; a healthy transformer at rated load is warm, not overheated.
distractorExplanations.b: An open safety on Y drops load off the secondary, so the transformer runs cooler, not hotter.
distractorExplanations.c: Serving 20 VA from 40 VA is half load; extra unused VA capacity does not cause overheating.

nate-core-readiness-check-electrical-033.prompt: On a typical induced-draft gas furnace, when does the inducer motor run relative to ignition?

options.a: It pre-purges to prove draft, then runs through the burn as designed
options.b: It starts after flame is proven, pulling flue gas only once burners are lit
options.c: It runs only for the post-purge after the gas valve has already closed
options.d: It replaces the circulating blower and moves room air across the heat exchanger

nate-core-readiness-check-electrical-033.explanation: The inducer pre-purges and must close the pressure switch before the control allows trial-for-ignition. It then stays on through the burn and usually post-purges. It moves combustion products through the heat exchanger; the indoor blower, not the inducer, moves conditioned air.

distractorExplanations.b: Ignition is locked out until draft is proven; the inducer is already running before the spark or hot surface igniter.
distractorExplanations.c: Post-purge is only one slice of the cycle; the inducer also pre-purges and runs during the entire burn.
distractorExplanations.d: The circulating blower moves supply air; the inducer is a combustion-vent motor, not a room-air mover.

nate-core-readiness-check-electrical-034.prompt: A condensing-unit contactor has badly pitted, burned points and the compressor voltage sags when it pulls in. What is the correct repair?

options.a: File the points smooth and put the same contactor back in as routine service
options.b: Replace the contactor; pitted contacts add resistance and drop voltage
options.c: Leave it in place unless an ohmmeter shows the coil winding is open
options.d: Keep the pitted points and add a hard-start kit to overcome the sag

nate-core-readiness-check-electrical-034.explanation: Pitted contacts raise resistance, drop voltage at the compressor terminals, and keep arcing. Replacement is the repair. Filing strips the silver facing and is only a short-term field patch. Coil continuity does not prove the power contacts are good, and a hard-start kit hides the voltage drop while the points keep burning.

distractorExplanations.a: Filing removes the contact plating and is a temporary patch; badly pitted contactors are replaced.
distractorExplanations.c: Coil continuity does not measure contact resistance; pitted power points can still drop voltage with a good coil.
distractorExplanations.d: A hard-start kit adds torque but leaves the high-resistance contacts in the circuit to keep degrading.

nate-core-readiness-check-electrical-035.prompt: A compressor uses a start capacitor with a potential relay. When should that start capacitor stay in the circuit?

options.a: Continuously, in series with the start winding the same way a run capacitor is used
options.b: Through start and run, left paralleled with the run capacitor for the whole cycle
options.c: Only during start, then dropped out by the relay or PTC once the motor is up
options.d: Only after the motor is at speed, so it can correct running power factor

nate-core-readiness-check-electrical-035.explanation: Start capacitors are intermittent-duty. A potential relay or PTC takes them out of the circuit once the motor approaches speed. Left in during run they overheat and fail. Continuous phase shift and power-factor correction are the run capacitor’s job, not the start capacitor’s.

distractorExplanations.a: That wiring describes a run capacitor; start capacitors are not continuous-duty and fail if left in circuit.
distractorExplanations.b: A hard-start kit parallels the run capacitor only for start; it must drop out or the start capacitor cooks.
distractorExplanations.d: Running power-factor correction is the run capacitor’s role; the start capacitor adds torque during start only.

nate-core-readiness-check-electrical-036.prompt: You are wiring a new heat-pump thermostat and need to know when the reversing-valve solenoid is energized. What is the right check?

options.a: Assume heating on every brand because the valve fails safe into cooling
options.b: Feed the solenoid 240 V from the contactor so it tracks compressor run
options.c: Energize it in both modes; defrost simply turns the solenoid off to reverse flow
options.d: Energize it in one mode and confirm O versus B on the OEM diagram

nate-core-readiness-check-electrical-036.explanation: Most split heat pumps energize the reversing valve in cooling (thermostat O). Some brands energize in heating (B). The solenoid is a 24 V coil, not a line-voltage load on the contactor. Read the outdoor-unit diagram rather than guessing fail-safe polarity.

distractorExplanations.a: Some OEMs use B (energize in heat), but many use O (energize in cool); fail-safe polarity is not universal.
distractorExplanations.b: The reversing-valve coil is 24 V from O/B, not 240 V paralleled with the compressor contactor.
distractorExplanations.c: The valve is powered in only one mode; defrost drives it to the cooling position, which may be on or off by brand.

nate-core-readiness-check-electrical-037.prompt: A furnace board flashes a pressure-switch fault on a call for heat and never tries ignition. What should you check first?

options.a: Inducer operation, vent and intake, and the hose to the pressure switch
options.b: The flame rod, treating the flash as a failed flame-prove after ignition
options.c: The high-limit switch and blower wheel, as if the code were a limit trip
options.d: Gas-valve outlet pressure on a manometer before looking at the vent

nate-core-readiness-check-electrical-037.explanation: A pressure-switch fault means the control did not see the inducer prove draft. Check inducer spin, blocked or disconnected vent/intake, a cracked or water-logged hose, and the switch itself. Flame sense, limits, and gas pressure are later in the sequence and are not energized until the switch closes.

distractorExplanations.b: The flame sensor proves flame after ignition; this code is about draft proof before the trial for ignition.
distractorExplanations.c: A high-limit trip is a different code; a pressure-switch fault points at the inducer and vent path.
distractorExplanations.d: The gas valve is not powered until the pressure switch closes, so manometer work skips the draft circuit.

nate-core-readiness-check-electrical-038.prompt: A clamp meter on a compressor run lead shows locked-rotor amps that never fall after the contactor closes. What does that mean?

options.a: Normal inrush that is allowed to sit at LRA for a couple of minutes
options.b: The compressor or outdoor fan is not starting; the rotor is locked
options.c: A high-efficiency scroll drawing full-load current that looks like LRA
options.d: A normal current spike while the heat pump is in an active defrost

nate-core-readiness-check-electrical-038.explanation: Locked-rotor amps last only for a fraction of a second on a successful start, then current falls toward RLA. LRA that holds means the rotor is not turning: open start circuit, failed capacitor, or a seized compressor or fan. Kill power and diagnose before the windings overheat.

distractorExplanations.a: Healthy inrush collapses in well under a second; sustained LRA is a locked rotor, not a timed warm-up.
distractorExplanations.c: A motor at full load draws about RLA, which is far below locked-rotor amps on the nameplate.
distractorExplanations.d: Defrost does not pin the compressor at LRA; running current in defrost still sits near RLA.

nate-core-readiness-check-electrical-039.prompt: At a conventional 24 V thermostat sub-base, what do terminals R and C supply?

options.a: 24 V hot and the cooling call that drives the outdoor contactor coil
options.b: 120 V hot and neutral taken straight off the furnace transformer primary
options.c: 24 V hot and common from the control-transformer secondary
options.d: 24 V hot and the reversing-valve output used on heat-pump O or B

nate-core-readiness-check-electrical-039.explanation: R is the hot side of the 24 V transformer secondary and C is the common return. Powered thermostats and many controls need both. Y is the cooling call, O/B is reversing-valve, and 120 V belongs on the transformer primary—not on the thermostat terminals.

distractorExplanations.a: The cooling call to the contactor is Y; C is the common return of the 24 V secondary, not the Y output.
distractorExplanations.b: 120 V feeds the transformer primary; R and C are the 24 V secondary leads, not line voltage.
distractorExplanations.d: Reversing-valve output is O or B; C is the common side of the control circuit, not a valve feed.

nate-core-readiness-check-electrical-040.prompt: A furnace transformer secondary is described as floating (ungrounded). How should you treat the C connection?

options.a: Bond C to the suction line so refrigerant piping becomes the ground point
options.b: Leave C disconnected at the board so the secondary stays fully floating
options.c: Ground both R and C secondary legs to keep the 24 V circuit balanced
options.d: Follow the OEM grounding and C landing so safeties and Wi-Fi stats work

nate-core-readiness-check-electrical-040.explanation: “Floating” does not mean C is unused. Land common where the schematic shows, including any OEM chassis ground of one secondary leg. Powered thermostats and many flame/safety circuits need that defined common. Bonding to piping or grounding both legs creates faults.

distractorExplanations.a: Refrigerant piping is not a control-circuit grounding electrode; follow the furnace schematic, not the suction line.
distractorExplanations.b: C is still required for powered stats and many safeties; a floating secondary still uses its common lead.
distractorExplanations.c: Grounding both secondary legs shorts the transformer through earth and typically blows the 24 V fuse.

nate-core-readiness-check-electrical-041.prompt: An outdoor condensing unit hums when the contactor pulls in, but the compressor never starts. What should you check first?

options.a: Indoor filter loading only, treating the hum as a return-air restriction
options.b: The run or start capacitor and a possible seized compressor
options.c: Whether the liquid-line drier was installed with the flow arrow reversed
options.d: Suction-line insulation thickness before any electrical or amp test

nate-core-readiness-check-electrical-041.explanation: Hum-no-start is a classic open or weak capacitor or a locked compressor. Confirm voltage at the terminals, check capacitor µF, and feel whether the compressor is trying to turn. Airflow, driers, and insulation do not make a compressor hum in place of starting.

distractorExplanations.a: A dirty indoor filter can trip high pressure after a start, but it does not keep a humming compressor from starting.
distractorExplanations.c: A reversed drier is a restriction after the unit is running; it does not produce a hum-no-start at the compressor.
distractorExplanations.d: Suction insulation affects heat gain on the line; it is not a start-circuit or seized-rotor diagnosis.

nate-core-readiness-check-electrical-042.prompt: A heat-pump outdoor board is in defrost. What typically ends that defrost cycle?

options.a: The indoor coil sensor reaching a comfort termination temperature
options.b: Outdoor coil termination temperature or a time-limit backup
options.c: Outdoor air rising above the auxiliary-heat balance-point setting
options.d: The board’s 30/60/90-minute pin timing out while still in defrost

nate-core-readiness-check-electrical-042.explanation: Defrost ends when the outdoor coil (or liquid-line) sensor rises to the termination temperature, or when a time-limit backup expires if the coil stays cold. The indoor coil is not the defrosted surface. Balance point controls auxiliary heat, and the 30/60/90 pins set time between defrost checks, not the end of an active defrost.

distractorExplanations.a: Defrost clears ice from the outdoor coil; an indoor-coil temperature is not the termination input.
distractorExplanations.c: Balance point governs auxiliary-heat lockout and staging, not when an active defrost ends.
distractorExplanations.d: Those pins set the interval between defrost attempts, not the maximum length of the defrost that is already running.

nate-core-readiness-check-electrical-043.prompt: A communicating or PWM furnace ECM blower will not run on a call for heat even though line voltage is present at the motor. What is usually missing?

options.a: A run capacitor and speed taps on the motor’s line-voltage leads, as on a PSC
options.b: A separate variable-frequency drive mounted in the furnace control panel
options.c: An OEM PWM, serial, or 24 V tap command plus line voltage
options.d: Line voltage alone, with speed set only by an internal motor thermistor

nate-core-readiness-check-electrical-043.explanation: ECM modules need a command from the furnace control—PWM, serial, or discrete 24 V taps—plus correct line voltage and a good common. They do not use a PSC run capacitor. Drive electronics sit in the motor module, not a panel VFD, and line power by itself does not set torque or speed.

distractorExplanations.a: That describes a PSC blower; ECMs have no run capacitor and are commanded by a low-voltage or serial signal.
distractorExplanations.b: ECM inverter electronics are inside the motor end module; residential furnaces do not add a separate panel VFD.
distractorExplanations.d: Line voltage powers the module; without the control’s command signal the motor typically will not run.

nate-core-readiness-check-electrical-044.prompt: A new Wi-Fi thermostat keeps dropping offline on a furnace with no unused C conductor at the wall. What is the clean fix?

options.a: Jumper R to C at the thermostat so it can draw continuous 24 V power
options.b: Feed R and C from a plug-in 120 V adapter to power the Wi-Fi radio
options.c: Replace the batteries and treat C as optional backup for the display
options.d: Add a C wire or an approved power extender per the OEM docs

nate-core-readiness-check-electrical-044.explanation: Wi-Fi stats need a real 24 V common. Run a C wire, use a spare conductor, or install an OEM-approved power extender / common maker. Jumping R to C shorts the transformer. 120 V on R/C destroys the control. Batteries do not stop power-stealing dropouts.

distractorExplanations.a: Jumping R to C shorts the 24 V secondary and typically blows the control fuse or the transformer.
distractorExplanations.b: R and C are 24 V control terminals; applying 120 V destroys the thermostat and often the furnace board.
distractorExplanations.c: C supplies continuous 24 V for the radio; batteries do not keep a power-stealing Wi-Fi thermostat online.

nate-core-readiness-check-electrical-045.prompt: You are installing a fused disconnect at a split-system condensing unit. How should the fuse size be chosen?

options.a: From the unit nameplate maximum fuse or HACR breaker rating
options.b: Equal to the minimum circuit ampacity printed on the nameplate
options.c: At 125 percent of compressor RLA, ignoring the outdoor fan motor
options.d: Equal to the compressor locked-rotor amps listed on the nameplate

nate-core-readiness-check-electrical-045.explanation: Overcurrent protection at the condensing unit follows the nameplate maximum fuse or HACR circuit-breaker rating. Minimum circuit ampacity sizes the conductors, not the fuses. Using 125% of compressor RLA alone leaves out other loads, and fusing at LRA provides almost no protection.

distractorExplanations.b: MCA sizes the branch-circuit conductors; fuses are taken from the nameplate maximum overcurrent device.
distractorExplanations.c: 125% of RLA is part of the MCA wire-sizing math and is not the fuse or breaker rating by itself.
distractorExplanations.d: LRA is far above the allowed overcurrent rating; fusing at LRA leaves the conductors essentially unprotected.
